analysis.one_liner: Blocks credit bureaus from selling mortgage shoppers' data to lenders without consent.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill with 93 cosponsors that would have stopped mortgage "trigger lead" sales of homebuyers' credit data died in the House Financial Services Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: When you apply for a home mortgage, credit bureaus can sell your information to other lenders within days, who then bombard you with calls and offers — these are called "trigger leads." This bill would stop that unless the lender got your documented consent, already made your loan, services it, or is a bank or credit union where you have an account. It was introduced with strong bipartisan support but never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Homebuyers and homeowners refinancing a mortgage. Today, the moment a lender pulls your credit for a mortgage, the credit bureaus can flag it and sell your name to any lender who asks, and many people get dozens of unsolicited calls. Under the bill, a bureau could only hand your report to a third party if that party certified it had your permission, already originated or services your loan, or is a bank or credit union holding your account [S2][S3]. Your own lender and existing bank relationships would be unaffected, so getting a mortgage stays as easy as it is now [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Ends 'trigger leads': credit reporting agencies could no longer furnish your credit report to unrelated third parties during a residential mortgage transaction unless that party certifies it has your consent, or already made or services your loan, or is an insured bank or credit union holding your account.
The consent requirement is documented — a third party must submit paperwork certifying your authorization — so it creates an auditable record rather than relying on lenders' word.

It does this by amending the existing Fair Credit Reporting Act prescreening rules, so it closes a specific loophole without touching ordinary credit checks for your own loan, credit cards, or employment.

analysis.who_pays: The three national credit bureaus, which sell trigger leads as a revenue product, lose that income stream. Independent (non-bank) mortgage lenders and lead brokers that buy trigger leads to solicit borrowers lose their main channel for reaching people shopping for a mortgage. Neither industry bears any cost beyond lost marketing access — there is no enforcement fund or penalty scheme directed at ordinary people.
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit bureaus and mortgage lead sellers

drawbacks.text: The bill carves out banks and credit unions: they can keep pulling reports on their own account holders without fresh consent, while independent mortgage companies that rely on trigger leads to compete for borrowers lose that channel. That tilts the mortgage market toward depository banks.

Some borrowers benefit from trigger leads: unsolicited offers can introduce competition for your loan, and some shoppers get better rates because multiple lenders bid. This bill shrinks that pool of competing offers to the lenders you contacted or already bank with.
The bill only restricts reports furnished during mortgage transactions, so credit bureaus' broader practice of packaging and selling consumer data for other credit products continues untouched.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy benefit is real but modest in dollars: this stops a well-known annoyance — a flood of sales calls after you apply for a mortgage — not a financial hardship. The main cost falls on lenders' marketing budgets and bureau revenue, though a genuine trade-off is that some borrowers who benefited from competing unsolicited offers will see fewer of them. The design's biggest flaw is the bank carve-out, which protects depositories' access while cutting off non-bank competitors. On balance a reasonable consumer-protection measure, but a narrow one.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Rose (R-TN) introduced the Homebuyers Privacy Protection Act on February 7, 2024, with a bipartisan group of original cosponsors including Rep. Ritchie Torres (D-NY).
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services — the only action the bill ever received.
The bill gathered 93 cosponsors, split 51 Republicans and 42 Democrats, showing broad two-party support, but the committee never took it up.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died in committee without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit bureaus and the lenders who buy trigger leads are better off, because they keep selling homebuyers' information without restriction. The bipartisan sponsors and the homebuyers they aimed to protect got nothing.

for.name: Rep. John Rose
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a bipartisan group of original cosponsors

for.name: Rep. Ritchie Torres
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship from day one

for.what_they_did: Signed on in support across both parties

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership (Chair Patrick McHenry)

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup during the 118th Congress, leaving it to die in committee

against.name: Credit bureau industry (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion via their trade group)
against.what_they_did: Have lobbied against trigger-lead restrictions, which are a revenue product for the bureaus

sides.party_line_note: Support was genuinely bipartisan — 93 cosponsors split 51 Republicans and 42 Democrats — so the bill's failure was not a party-line vote but a committee that never acted.

industries.note: Trigger leads — flagging a mortgage credit pull and selling the shopper's data to any lender who pays — are a direct revenue product. The bill shuts that product off for mortgage transactions unless the buyer certifies consent.

industries.industry: Non-bank mortgage lenders and lead brokers
industries.note: These firms use trigger leads as their primary way to reach people shopping for a mortgage; the bill removes that channel. For borrowers it removes sales calls, but also some competing offers.

The bill expressly exempts insured depositories and credit unions holding a consumer's account, so they keep pulling reports on existing customers without fresh consent — an advantage over independent mortgage competitors the bill does restrict.
